results.title: Guideline of the Week - by Emergency Medicine Update
results.content:
Title: Guideline of the Week - by Emergency Medicine Update
# Guideline of the Week. ### Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026 — SCCM/ESICM (March 2026). The bag of 0.9% saline. The qSOFA score on the whiteboard. The three-hour antibiotic target on every sepsis proforma. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign just told us to reconsider all of it. Published March 2026, the SSC’s latest adult guidelines are the most substantial update since 2021 — 129 statements, 46 of them brand new, published simultaneously in Intensive Care Medicine and Critical Care Medicine and endorsed by 24 professional societies. The 2021 SSC guidelines moved away from rigid bundle targets, but five years of new evidence in fluid strategy, antibiotic optimisation, vasopressor timing, and screening tool performance had accumulated — applied inconsistently. Areas that stayed soft in 2021 — balanced crystalloids, prolonged beta-lactam infusions, peripheral vasopressor initiation — have been re-examined and, where evidence supports it, upgraded. ## New Guideline or Update? This is a major update, not a new document. The headline changes: balanced crystalloids are now recommended over 0.9% saline; prolonged beta-lactam infusions are now a recommendation rather than a suggestion; NEWS or NEWS2 is formally endorsed over qSOFA for screening; peripheral vasopressors are explicitly supported; antibiotic timing is stratified by severity; and MAP targets are age-stratified for the first time. For adults with sepsis or septic shock, balanced crystalloids (Hartmann’s, Plasma-Lyte) are now formally recommended over 0.9% saline. The SMART trial sepsis subgroup showed 31.2% vs 26.3% in-hospital mortality in favour of balanced crystalloids. This deliberately moves away from a blanket one-hour target for all patients — a change designed to reduce empiric over-prescribing in undifferentiated presentations. The BLING III trial was neutral on 90-day mortality but showed improved clinical cure; a subsequent meta-analysis confirmed a mortality benefit. An initial MAP target of 60–65 mmHg is now suggested over the standard ≥65 mmHg in older patients with septic shock. The 65 trial showed no increase in 90-day mortality with permissive hypotension in this group, with lower vasopressor doses and no additional adverse events. *Based on Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026 — Evans et al., Intensive Care Medicine / Critical Care Medicine, March 2026.

# GRACE-2

[Home](/)   /  [Publications](/publications)   /  [GRACE](/publications/grace)   /  GRACE-2

![GRACE w tag logo](/images/default-source/logos/grace-w-tag-logo.png?sfvrsn=80a3730d_0 "GRACE w tag logo")

The SAEM GRACE program addresses the best practices for the care of the most common chief complaints that can be seen on the tracking board of any emergency department in the country, based upon research and expert consensus. These guidelines are designed with de-implementation as a guiding principle to reasonably reduce wasteful testing, provide explicit criteria to reduce foreseeable risk, and define sensible and prudent medical care.

#### [GRACE-2: Low-Risk, Recurrent Abdominal Pain in the Emergency Department](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/acem.14495)

Abdominal pain has consistently remained the most frequent chief complaint in United States emergency departments (EDs) from 2009 to 2018. The evaluation of acute abdominal pain requires substantial ED resources, including imaging, laboratory studies, nursing care, time, and patient care space. Despite the intensity of diagnostic testing, most patients presenting with abdominal pain do not receive a specific diagnosis in the ED and are discharged.

National data on ED presentations for recurrent abdominal pain are limited. Little guidance is available to emergency physicians evaluating and treating patients with recurrent and undifferentiated abdominal pain. Without guidelines for care, variance in practice could result in lower quality care, including risks of over- or under-testing, misdiagnosis, adverse effects of over- or under-treatment, higher costs, greater length of stay, and lower patient satisfaction.

The purpose of the second Guideline for Reasonable and Appropriate Care in the Emergency Department (GRACE-2) is to provide an evidence-based, patient-centric approach for clinicians in their evaluation and management of adult patients with low-risk, recurrent, undifferentiated abdominal pain in the ED.   
  
The GRACE-2 panel reached the following recommendations:

1. If a prior negative computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis (CTAP) has been performed within 12 months, there is insufficient evidence to accurately identify populations in whom repeat CTAP imaging can be safely avoided or routinely recommended.
2. If CTAP with IV contrast is negative, the panel suggests against ultrasound unless there is concern for pelvic or biliary pathology.
3. The panel suggests screening for depression and/or anxiety may be performed during the ED evaluation.
4. The panel suggests using an opioid-minimizing strategy for pain control.

##### Read the full article:  [GRACE-2: Low-Risk, Recurrent Abdominal Pain in the Emergency Department](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/acem.14495)

Ministry of Health, Rwanda   (2022)  C1

Emergency medicine in Rwanda is underdeveloped. Limited training and infrastructure mean that the country has a high mortality rate from acute conditions such as trauma, malaria and obstetric complications. As Rwanda's disease burden shifts, there is a critical need for standardised emergency care. This Emergency Medicine Clinical Guideline (EMCG) provides essential protocols and principles that are tailored to the Rwandan context. The aim is to improve the delivery of emergency care at district and referral hospitals. It is intended as a practical resource for all healthcare providers involved in the management of undifferentiated emergencies.

Title: Clinical Practice Guideline for Emergency... : Annals of Emergency Medicine
Pain management and sedation/concept. # **Clinical Practice Guideline for Emergency Department Ketamine Dissociative Sedation: 2011 Update**. Annals of Emergency Medicine 57(5):p 449-461, May 2011. We update an evidence-based clinical practice guideline for the administration of the dissociative agent ketamine for emergency department procedural sedation and analgesia. Substantial new research warrants revision of the widely disseminated 2004 guideline, particularly with respect to contraindications, age recommendations, potential neurotoxicity, and the role of coadministered anticholinergics and benzodiazepines. We critically discuss indications, contraindications, personnel requirements, monitoring, dosing, coadministered medications, recovery issues, and future research questions for ketamine dissociative sedation.
